highlights.text: The root's base meaning is "the small newborn."
A male child is طِفْل (ṭifl), a female طِفْلَة (ṭiflah).
while over the earth lay the shadows of the ṭafal.
two genuine underlying senses that he thinks may ultimately converge
He cites Q48:24 (al-Fatḥ), "after He had given you victory over them" (aẓfarakum ʿalayhim), as a Qur'anic instance of this usage.
ẓufr = the human fingernail.
kalīl al-ẓufur, "blunt of nail" — Ibn Fāris cites a line of Ṭarafa's poetry using this image
one sound, regular root whose meaning is movement over the ground that is lighter than walking
Everything that walks on the earth is a dābba.
He cites Imruʾ al-Qays: "When she comes forward, you would say: a green gourd dipped in the pools."
A line by al-Hudhalī is cited: "on his side a creeping wound that spills over."
"Neither a daybūb nor a qallāʿ will enter the Garden."
one root whose core idea is softness, ease, and a small quantity
الدُّهْن (duhn) is oil or grease
الْمُدَاهَنَة (mudāhana) is مُصَانَعَة, humouring or accommodating someone
cites Q 68:9, "they wished that you would be pliant, so they too would be pliant."
a single, regularly patterned root whose core sense is entering, going in, penetration (wulūj)
دَخَلَ = "he entered."
cited with a line of al-Hudhalī on "an interleaved drinking (shurb dikhāl)."
one sound root whose single idea is emptiness together with breadth of scope
الفَرَاغ (farāgh) is the opposite of being busy.
أَفْرَغَ (afragha) = to pour water out
Ibn Fāris states the usage is figurative, on the ground that God is not occupied by one matter to the exclusion of another.
He reports that the exegetes glossed sa-nafrughu as نَعْمِدُ ("We shall set about / turn deliberately to")
al-fūm — crop/grain or wheat generally
a line of poetry by Abū Miḥjan al-Thaqafī about not needing to cultivate fūm
a line by Umayyah listing fūmān among garden produce
some exegetes read fūm as "garlic," treating the fāʾ as a substitution for thāʾ
insist al-fūm means wheat/grain, arguing it would be absurd for the Israelites to request food with no wheat
a single sound root meaning one thing containing or enveloping another
a guarantor or surety (ḍāmin); verb كَفَلَ بِهِ (to stand surety), verbal noun كَفَالَة
He cites the Qur'anic وَكَفَّلَهَا زَكَرِيَّا (Āl ʿImrān 37), "He put her in Zakariyyā's charge."
Ibn Fāris cites a verse ("He grew exhausted, so we slung him… and bound him fast above")
A ḥadīth applies the word to the broken notch of a vessel, calling it "Satan's kifl."
is not built on one underlying analogy, and its words come from separate origins
quṭr is a side or quarter; the plural aqṭār means the flanks or sides of a thing.
qaṭirān (tar), which he suggests may be named from dripping
Cited from Ṭarafa: the people in their assembly call out asking whether what they smell is the smoke of roasting meat (qutār)
one sound root with a single core idea: something taken/seized, and a drawing-together or gathering-in within a thing
قَبَضْتُ الشَّيْءَ (qabaḍtu al-shayʾ) — "I took/received the thing,"
His Qurʾānic shāhid is Q 67:19, on the birds overhead "spreading [their wings] and drawing them in"
Poetic witness from Ruʾbah: "a brisk driver, between the rough-handed and the deft."
one sound root whose core idea is **something obscured or hidden, together with lowness / sinking down**
القَبْر (al-qabr) is the grave of a dead person
the verb shifts to the fourth form أَقْبَرَ (aqbara).
The place of graves is مَقْبَرَة or مَقْبُرَة (maqbara / maqbura)
He cites al-Aʿshā as the poetic witness: had she leaned a dead man against her breast, he would have revived
He reports that some exegetes read فَأَقْبَرَهُ in that verse as meaning that man was *inspired/taught how burial is done*
a single sound root whose core sense is precedence and forward motion
الْقِدَم is the opposite of coming-newly-into-being (حُدوث). A قَدِيم thing is one whose time is past.
قَدَمُ صِدْقٍ ("a foot of truth") means a prior record of good repute.
قَدَم (the human foot) is well known
illustrated by a line of al-Quṭāmī.
one sound root meaning the extent, essence, and limit of a thing
al-qadr = the extent or amount of anything (qadruhu kadhā = "its measure is such")
In Q 65:7 (man qudira ʿalayhi rizquhu) qudira means qutira, "was straitened" — given provision in scant measure.
In Q 6:91 (mā qadarū llāha ḥaqqa qadrihi) the exegetes gloss "they did not magnify God with His true greatness"
two sound roots: (1) joining one thing to another, and (2) something protruding with strength
a generation/nation of people; plural قُرُون. Cites Q 25:38 ("many generations between that").
مُقْرِن لكذا = equal to / able for something.
which al-Aṣmaʿī explained as their long hair (with a verse of Muraqqish)
a burst of sweat; plural قُرُون (with a verse of Zuhayr)
a genuine root whose core idea is gathering together and narrowing/restricting
to be tight-fisted with one's household.
he cites Yūnus 10:26, "no qatar nor abasement shall overcast their faces."
Ṭarafa's line in which people in their assembly ask whether what they smell is roasting meat (qutār)
one root with a single core idea: **binding/fastening, and the firmness that results from it**
رَبَطَ / يَرْبِطُ / رَبْط — to tie a thing.
رَابِطُ الْجَأْشِ = a man firm of heart and self-command.
Labīd: "steadfast of heart at the gap in their line
Ibn Aḥmar: "firmer of heart in defence of his people's notables
a single core idea: **a coming-together**, of people or of other things
Al-rahṭ names a group of men numbering from three up to ten.
A verse of poetry laments a war that "laid low bands of men (arāhiṭ), and so they found rest"
a coming and going — setting out in a single direction, moving back and forth
رَاوَدْتُهُ (rāwadtuhu) — to press or coax someone toward doing something; to urge him to it.
إِرَادَة (irādah, "wanting/will") derives from the wāw of this root
ruwaydan) — doing an action gently, slowly.
جَارِيَةٌ رُودٌ (jāriyatun rūd) — a young woman; illustrated by a verse
jamal siddiyy / ibil sadā — a stray/untended camel or camels left to roam; qawm sadā — an unsupervised, aimless people
"qad asdaytu fa-alḥim, wa asrajtu fa-aljim" — a proverb urging one to finish what's begun
"mā anta bi-laḥmatin wa lā sadāh" — "you are neither weft nor warp," an idiom for someone who neither helps nor harms.
a single root meaning to stay put, to remain in place with respect to something
وَقَفَ / يَقِفُ / وُقُوف (waqafa, yaqifu, wuqūf) — to stand, to halt.
His evidence is a line of al-Ṭirimmāḥ: "headlong in my error, then I desisted, content with mindful restraint — and the man of piety is content."
two separate roots: one about good things and wealth, whose origin is the leafage of a tree, and one about a colour
waraq — the leaves of a tree.
riqa — silver coin (dirhams).
Two distinct roots gathered under this spelling
al-khuḍūʿ — humility, self-abasement; ikhtaḍaʿa — he humbled himself
khaḍaʿa/akhḍaʿa — of a man's speech, to soften it
al-khaḍaʿ (per al-Shaybānī) — bending the neck toward the chest, applied to a camel (Zuhayr's poetry)
one whose head droops toward its snout, illustrated with a line of poetry by al-Nābighah
a hadith citation applies this to forbidding a man from speaking softly/suggestively to a woman not his own
a single root (aṣl wāḥid) with closely related branches, all of which, he says, go back either to **thinness** (diqqa) or to a **gap** (furja)
Ibn Fāris places al-khalīl, the one who is your close friend (yukhālluka), under this sense
Al-khalal is the space between two things.
one root whose single origin lies in the domain of number
خَمْسَة (five) is well known; الخُمْس is one part out of five, a fifth.
خَمَسْتُهم also means "I was the fifth of them."
supported by a line of al-Aʿshā contrasting a thing that looks "like the cloaks of al-Khims" one day and spoiled hide the next.
Ibn Fāris also quotes Muʿādh telling the people of Yemen to bring "a khamīs or a labīs" garment to be taken from them as ṣadaqah.
He cites the report that when the Prophet came in sight of Khaybar the people called out "Muḥammad — and the khamīs!", meaning the army.
a single root whose core meaning is diminution / detraction (al-tanaqquṣ) — taking something away, falling short
is to act treacherously or faithlessly toward someone — which he defines as a deficiency of fidelity (a falling-short of loyalty)
He cites Dhū al-Rumma on an abode "worn down / eroded" at times by cloud and at times by a hot, dusty west wind (bāriḥ)
